transcript:
Header: 2026-08-27 16:00 UTC | Duration: ~58 min | Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Carlos (Redwood SE), Jared (Acme Platform), Priya (Acme Security), Evelyn (Acme SRE)

Summary (auto-gen, may be rough): go into privatelink vs peering, NAT egress for model pulls, dns resolution, kv cache warming, benchmarks, next steps.

[00:00] Maya: hey everyone thanks for joining, uh real quick intros, i'm maya from redwood, carlos is our runtime se, go ahead carlos.
[00:12] Carlos: hi all, yeah i'll be driving the deep dive - we'll look at networking topologies and how that impacts p95 p99 and throughput.
[00:20] Jared: thanks, quick context - acme runs prod in AWS us-east-1, we have restrictive egress, we use multiple private subnets and a central NAT for outbound, and security needs us to avoid public endpoints if possible.
[00:35] Priya: SOC2 requirements, need to see audit logs, we prefer KMS backed keys, and anything that touches customer data needs to stay in VPC or private link.
[00:48] Evelyn: SRE here - latency SLO is p95 < 250ms for our synchronous endpoints, but we'll accept slightly higher for complex prompts. Also want deterministic cold start behavior.

[00:58] Carlos: ok first slide - two patterns we see: interface endpoints (AWS PrivateLink) and VPC peering / transit gateway. PrivateLink gives you interface ENIs in your subnets that route to Redwood's private endpoint, peering gives direct routing but needs route table updates and we often need NAT for internet-bound model pulls.
[01:25] Maya: important nuance: PrivateLink keeps control plane traffic private and avoids exposing public IPs on runtime nodes. For many customers it's the security-friendly option.
[01:38] Jared: right, question: what about DNS? If we put a privatelink endpoint, how does the model registry hostname resolve inside our VPC?
[01:46] Carlos: good question. With PrivateLink we provide a service name that you create an AWS Endpoint for; AWS will create interface ENIs and you can configure private hosted zone entries or rely on the endpoint's DNS. Sometimes customers use split-horizon with Route53 inbound/outbound rules, other times they add an alias record. There's a caveat: some SDKs cache DNS aggressively which can cause stale endpoints after failover.
[02:10] Priya: so we need guaranteed DNS failover testing - if the primary AZ with the ENI degrades, we must not see long TTL-caused errors.
[02:18] Carlos: yes, we recommend short TTLs for endpoint records and client-side retry with exponential backoff. Also health checks on the interface endpoints; Redwood can advertise multi-AZ endpoints so failover is quick.
[02:35] Evelyn: what about NAT egress - our cluster can't access S3 or internet except via central NAT. Does Redwood need to download models at startup? How do you handle model pulls in Private mode?
[02:47] Maya: two options - you can prestage model artifacts into your private object storage (S3 in the VPC) and Redwood runtime will load from there, or allow Redwood's runtime nodes temporary egress to Redwood model registry via a NAT. For regulated customers we prefer prestaging.
[03:05] Carlos: prestaging is common: we provide an artifact manifest and signatures; you push the quantized shards into a customer bucket and runtime reads them locally. That avoids outbound egress and fits strict compliance. But prestaging introduces deployment complexity and requires orchestrating cache warm-up.
[03:25] Jared: cache warm-up, yep - how does KV cache interact - we rely on kv cache to avoid recomputation between requests, is that local to pod or shared?
[03:33] Carlos: current architecture uses per-runtime KV cache in memory; we also support a shared redis-backed KV for certain patterns but that increases network hops. For best latency p95, local in-memory KV cache is ideal. The tradeoff is cold-starts: when a node starts it has empty KV and first few requests see cold latency.
[03:55] Evelyn: can we pre-warm the KV cache? e.g., run synthetic requests once the node is up?
[04:01] Carlos: yes, we provide tooling to prime the cache. Two strategies: snake-like prefix prefetch (walk common prefixes) or replay short sets of historical prompts. Both need model weights present locally; if you're prestaging, priming happens faster. If the node needs to download shards over NAT, priming will be slow.
[04:20] Priya: about model shards - are downloads TLS authenticated? do they go through public internet?
[04:27] Maya: downloads always run over TLS and signed URLs or IAM role-based access when using S3. If using PrivateLink with prestaged S3 in the VPC, downloads are fully internal. If using Redwood-hosted registry, we recommend setting up PrivateLink so those downloads never traverse public internet.
[04:44] Jared: ok good. Next: subnets and endpoint placement. We have isolated subnets for compute in three AZs, and one central NAT in our management VPC. Where should interface endpoints be placed for minimal latency?
[04:57] Carlos: place interface endpoints into the same private subnets where your inference pods run. That avoids cross-AZ hops. Also ensure security groups on the ENIs allow the pod CIDR. If you have multiple AZs, create endpoints in each AZ.
[05:13] Maya: another tip: avoid routing traffic through a NAT for north-south inference calls - that adds extra latency. PrivateLink keeps it inside the VPC fabric.
[05:23] Evelyn: curious about TLS termination - does Redwood terminate TLS at the interface endpoint? How does mTLS work?
[05:30] Carlos: Redwood supports mTLS for node-to-control-plane and can do client certs for mutual auth. For PrivateLink, the connection terminates at the endpoint and then traffic goes to Redwood's internal network; we use TLS end-to-end. For extra assurance we can layer application-level mTLS between your runtime and our control-plane service.
[05:50] Priya: fine, also need audit logs. Will Redwood provide request-level audit logs and tokenization metadata?
[05:57] Maya: yes we can ship audit logs to your S3 or Splunk via a private ingestion path; logs can include request id, model version, timestamp, and anonymized metadata. We'll include details in the security pack.
[06:10] Jared: moving to performance — what are typical p95 numbers inside a privatelink deployment for 2k token requests and for 8k token requests?
[06:19] Carlos: rough ballpark — for a single-socket A100-class node with our optimized runtime, 2k tokens could be p95 ~ 120-180ms depending on batching, 8k tokens might be 350-700ms. But that's strongly dependent on model, batch size, quantization (int8 vs fp16), and kv cache hit rate. We'll provide a more precise table.
[06:44] Evelyn: that's a big range. We need guaranteed numbers for SLA negotiation.
[06:48] Carlos: understood — we'll run targeted benchmarks with your typical prompts during the pilot and give p50/p95/p99 plus token throughput.
[06:55] Priya: quantization question - any caveats for accuracy/regression when using int8 in private deployments?
[07:02] Carlos: there are tradeoffs. Our optimize team curates quant profiles per model; int8 can reduce latency and memory by 2-4x but may introduce small quality deltas on edge cases. We recommend running a few eval prompts to check quality regression. For regulated workflows, sometimes customers keep fp16 for safety.
[07:20] Jared: what about batching inside the runtime - does PrivateLink change batching behavior?
[07:24] Carlos: no, batching is runtime-local. However network jitter can influence batching windows; low jitter inside VPC helps maintain deterministic batching latency. Also we expose batch policy knobs so you can cap max batch size or set max wait time to tune p95 vs throughput.
[07:41] Maya: note: for enterprise we often recommend a conservative max wait of 10ms and smaller batch sizes for latency-sensitive services. For high-throughput background jobs you can raise batch windows.
[07:52] Evelyn: can we force certain routes to use local node's cache replica vs global? We have multi-cluster topology.
[07:58] Carlos: right now, KV is per-node by default. We can configure a shared Redis-like store but that adds ~1-2ms depending on placement. For multi-cluster, you can route traffic to a specific cluster via route tables or use a weighted routing fallback. We also support sticky sessions for a short TTL to improve cache hit rates.
[08:17] Priya: sticky sessions sound risky - session affinity could cause hotspots.
[08:20] Carlos: agreed, only recommend short TTLs and with autoscaling safety. We can instrument metrics to show cache hit distribution.
[08:29] Maya: ok lemme show a quick sketch (shared screen note: /s/privatelink-arch.png). This diagram shows interface ENIs in each AZ, runtime nodes in private subnets, optional NAT for outbound, and a prestaged S3 bucket with bucket policy allowing only your VPC.
[08:46] Jared: perfect - in that diagram, where do we plug in our egress firewall for outbound logs?
[08:51] Carlos: logs to your S3 can use VPC endpoint gateway for S3. If you need to route logs to external SIEM, we can send via private peering or use a logging collector inside your VPC that forwards outbound through approved channels.
[09:05] Evelyn: any recommendations about ENI limits? we have account-level ENI limits per AZ.
[09:10] Carlos: good call — interface endpoints create an ENI per AZ per service. For large fleets you should check ENI and IP address capacity; one pattern is to place endpoints in shared subnets with larger CIDRs, or use VPC peering for scale. We'll share a checklist for subnet sizing.
[09:28] Priya: security: KMS integration - can Redwood support customer-managed keys (CMKs) for model encryption at rest?
[09:35] Maya: yes, customer-managed KMS is supported for S3 buckets and we can integrate with HSM for private deploys. We'll include the KMS workflow in the security doc.
[09:45] Jared: edge case - what if our NAT is stateful and we experience port exhaustion when multiple nodes download shards?
[09:52] Carlos: that happens. Solutions: use S3 VPC gateway endpoints for internal transfers (no NAT), stagger downloads with backoff, or increase NAT capacity / use multiple NAT gateways. Prestaging avoids the issue.
[10:07] Evelyn: about certificate rotation for mTLS - how is that handled for long-running nodes?
[10:12] Carlos: we rotate certs via a CA-managed process; nodes pull new certs from the control plane over the private channel. Rotation is seamless with overlapping validity windows. We can also support your internal cert manager if you prefer.
[10:26] Priya: demo request - can we see a pilot run with our prompts and 8k tokens in a dedicated sandbox?
[10:32] Maya: yes — next steps: we'll provision a pilot in your staging VPC via PrivateLink, run benchmarks with your prompts, and provide full telemetry. I'll send a provisioning checklist after this call.
[10:42] Jared: timing? we want pilot before end of September.
[10:45] Maya: doable - we'll target week of Sept 13 for bench runs; need CIDRs and a contact to give infra access.
[10:52] Carlos: final notes on debugging - if you see spikes, please capture tcpdump + runtime logs; network path MTU issues have shown up in some customer's setups and can cause retransmits which inflate p95. Also, ensure path between pod and ENI doesn't cross a NAT device.
[11:10] Evelyn: good point. Also any suggestions for monitoring - what metrics does Redwood expose for privatelink deployments?
[11:16] Carlos: we export token-level latency histograms, kv-cache hit rates, model shard download durations, and endpoint health. Metrics can be pushed to your Prometheus via remote-write or we can push to CloudWatch.
[11:30] Priya: ok let's recap next steps.
[11:33] Maya: recap: Maya will share architecture diagram, CloudFormation sample, and security pack (SOC2, KMS/HSM notes). Carlos will do performance table and quantization guidance + run bench with Acme prompts. Jared will share CIDRs and confirm whether prestaging or runtime downloads are preferred. Schedule pilot week of 2026-09-13.
[11:54] Jared: sounds good, thanks.
[11:57] Maya: thanks everyone, we'll follow up in email with links and the checklist.
[12:01] call end.
